summary: Describes the Message Session Relay Protocol, used to send a series of related instant messages as part of a session. Message sessions are set up like any other media stream through a protocol such as SIP. It is a standards-track protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: MSRP carries related instant messages as part of a session negotiated through a signaling protocol such as SIP. The session lets the endpoints exchange content and request delivery reports, while leaving session setup to SIP and SDP.

subtitle: How SIP-set-up sessions carry related messages between participants over TCP.

tldr.problem: Separate instant messages do not by themselves establish a conversation with a negotiated start, end, and relationship to other media.
tldr.mechanism: MSRP carries MIME content in framed SEND and REPORT requests over TCP. SIP and SDP exchange session addresses and acceptable content types; SEND can divide a message into byte-range chunks.
tldr.outcome: MSRP defines peer-to-peer message sessions, while relays are specified separately in RFC 4976. RFC 4975 has been updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8591, RFC 8873, and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4975 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has been updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8591, RFC 8873, and RFC 8996; relay behavior is specified in RFC 4976.

sections.title: Message Sessions and Their Setup
sections.content:
A message session groups related messages into a conversation with a definite beginning and end. This differs from page-mode messaging, where each message is handled independently. RFC 4975 defines the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) as a transport for session-mode messages.

MSRP is not a standalone session-setup protocol. A rendezvous mechanism must exchange the endpoints' MSRP URIs, protect their confidentiality, support negotiation of incompatible extensions, and carry im: URIs. The RFC describes using Session Description Protocol (SDP) through a signaling protocol such as SIP. It covers peer-to-peer sessions crossing one hop; relay behavior is specified separately in RFC 4976.
sections.plainLanguage: MSRP groups messages into a conversation that has a negotiated start and end. SIP and SDP arrange the session and give each endpoint the address it should use.

sections.title: Negotiating and Opening a Session
sections.content:
Each endpoint includes an MSRP URI and acceptable content types in its SDP offer or answer. The required path attribute carries one or more URIs; the URI includes an explicit port. An endpoint without relays normally gives one URI, but it must be ready to receive a path with several.

The endpoint that sent the original offer opens the TCP connection when needed and immediately sends a SEND request. That first request binds the connection to the session. MSRP defines SEND to carry a complete message or part of one, and REPORT to communicate the status of a previously sent message or byte range.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints exchange addresses and state which content types they can accept. The original offerer opens the connection and sends the first request to identify the session.

sections.title: Request Framing and Message Boundaries
sections.content:
An MSRP request begins with a method and transaction identifier, followed by path headers and other fields. A request body requires a Content-Type field, placed last in the headers; a bodyless request has no content-type field or separating blank line. The end-line contains seven hyphens, the same transaction identifier, and a flag.

The final flag is a dollar sign when this is the end of a complete message, a plus sign when more data follows, and a number sign when the sender aborts an incomplete message. The sender must ensure that the end-line does not occur in the body. The transaction identifier must not collide with another active transaction and must include at least 64 bits of randomness.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request has a start and an end that share a transaction identifier. Its final character tells the receiver whether the message is complete, continues later, or has been stopped.

sections.title: Sending Large Messages in Chunks
sections.content:
A complete message may be divided among several SEND requests. Each chunk carries the same Message-ID; its Byte-Range identifies the positions it covers in the full message. Positions start at one. The receiver uses these values to place chunk data into the message, but must not assume that chunks arrive in order.

A chunk larger than 2048 octets must be interruptible, so it can give other sessions using the same TCP connection a chance to send data. The sender marks an interruptible range with an asterisk as its end. Relays may split or combine chunks, and overlapping data is handled according to the receiver's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Long messages can travel in separately numbered parts. The receiver uses each part's message ID and byte positions to assemble the message, even if parts arrive in a different order.

sections.title: Transaction Responses and Delivery Reports
sections.content:
A transaction response reports whether the next hop accepted a request. A delivery report describes the later outcome of a message. The sender controls reports with Success-Report and Failure-Report; if absent, success reporting defaults to no and failure reporting to yes.

With failure reporting set to yes, the sender must inform the user that delivery probably failed if no 200 response arrives within 30 seconds after the last byte is sent. With partial, the sender need not run that timer but still reports non-recoverable errors. With no, the receiver sends neither a failure REPORT nor a transaction response. A success REPORT may cover the whole message or a range of bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: A response confirms what happened on the current connection, while a REPORT can say whether the message was delivered. The sender can request success notices, failure notices, or no notices.

sections.title: Protecting Session Addresses and Messages
sections.content:
An MSRP URI is a shared secret during session setup. Its session identifier provides the secrecy and must contain at least 80 bits of randomness. A receiver checks that an incoming URI identifies an expected session and rejects a missing session with response 481.

Plain TCP does not protect the URI or message contents in transit. MSRP requires implementations to support TLS; an msrps URI requires TLS for that connection. For peer-to-peer TLS using self-signed certificates, the endpoints can exchange a certificate fingerprint in integrity-protected SDP and must end the session if it does not match. The RFC also warns that large byte-range values can cause excessive buffer allocation and recommends checking them before allocating memory.
sections.plainLanguage: The session address must be hard to guess and shared only through protected setup. TLS or signed and encrypted message content can protect traffic, and receivers should check byte ranges before reserving memory.
